subcategory: native coastal dune and bluff perennial

planting.note: Direct-sow scarified seed into loose, well-drained sand in early spring, or set out nursery plugs; germination is slow and erratic due to the hard, corky fruit coat.

directions: Yellow sand verbena is a trailing, fleshy-leaved perennial that forms loose mats over open sand on dunes and the lower, more mobile faces of coastal bluffs from British Columbia to central California. Plant in pure sand or sandy loam with excellent drainage and no supplemental fertility, since it is adapted to nutrient-poor, salt-sprayed substrates and rots in rich garden soil. Rounded clusters of bright yellow, sweetly fragrant flowers open mainly in the evening from late spring through summer and draw night-flying moths. Once established it needs only occasional deep watering and tolerates direct salt spray and burial by shifting sand.

subcategory: native coastal dune and bluff perennial legume

planting.note: Nick or lightly sand the hard seed coat and direct-sow into loose sandy soil once the ground is workable; this legume resents transplanting because of its deep taproot.

directions: Silky beach pea is a low, silvery-haired perennial found on open sand and the gravelly edges of rocky headlands along the Washington and Oregon outer coast, distinguished from inland beach peas by its dense silky pubescence that reflects sun and sheds salt spray. Its short, sprawling stems carry purple-pink pea flowers in spring, followed by flattened pods, and the root fixes nitrogen into the poor sandy soils it colonizes. Give it full sun, lean sandy or gravelly soil, and sharp drainage; it needs no fertilizer and little water once its taproot is established. Avoid rich, moisture-retentive beds, which encourage rot and floppy, untypical growth.

subcategory: native coastal dune and bluff perennial

planting.note: Direct-sow into loose sandy soil in spring; seedlings establish quickly and the trailing stems root as they spread, so division of rooted sections also works.

directions: Beach suncup is a gray-green, trailing mat-former that colonizes open sand on dunes and the sun-baked faces of coastal bluffs along the Pacific coast, with cup-shaped yellow flowers that age to orange-red and open through most of the warm season. Grow it in pure sand or sandy, fast-draining soil in full sun, mimicking the exposed, salt-sprayed foredune and bluff habitats where it naturally roots down at the stem nodes as it spreads. It needs very little irrigation once established and is a good small-scale sand stabilizer in a coastal garden. Cut back leggy growth after the main summer bloom to keep the mat tight.

subcategory: native coastal bluff and salt marsh annual

planting.note: Scatter seed over autumn into a patch already seeded or planted with a fine-rooted native grass or sedge host, since this species is a hemiparasite that needs root contact with a companion plant to thrive.

directions: Johnny-nip is a small, fleshy annual of coastal bluffs, headland turf, and the upper edges of salt marshes from British Columbia to Baja California, with cream-to-yellow bracted flower spikes often tipped in rose-purple. Like other paintbrushes it is a root hemiparasite, so sow it into an established stand of native grass, sedge, or low forb that it can tap into rather than alone in bare soil. It tolerates brief tidal splash and salt-laden fog and prefers soil that is seasonally damp in winter and spring but drier in summer. Leave seed heads in place to self-sow, since it is an annual that must reseed each year to persist in the planting.

planting.note: Plant container-grown saplings in spring in deep, well-drained, acidic soil at a site with cold winters and reliable snow cover; seed requires cold stratification and nursery propagation before field planting.

directions: California red fir forms dense, cathedral-like subalpine forests between roughly 6,000 and 9,000 feet in the Sierra Nevada and southern Cascades, just below the whitebark pine and mountain hemlock timberline belt, and is distinct from the Pacific Northwest's noble fir despite sharing the common nickname 'red fir.' It is named for its thick, reddish-brown, deeply furrowed bark on mature trunks and its stiff, upward-curving blue-green needles arranged densely around the twig. It needs cold winters with deep, insulating snowpack, acidic well-drained soil, and full sun once past the seedling stage, and is not suited to mild or dry low-elevation gardens. In cultivation it is used mainly as a large specimen conifer in high-elevation gardens and arboreta that can replicate its native cold, snowy conditions.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring into gritty, acidic, humus-rich soil that stays moist from snowmelt through early summer but drains well; avoid heavy clay or standing water.

directions: Brewer's mountain heather is a low, wiry evergreen shrub endemic to the Sierra Nevada and southern Cascades, forming mats on rocky slopes, talus, and timberline meadows just below true alpine fell-fields, where its bright rose-purple, bell-shaped flowers set it apart from the pink and cream-flowered mountain heathers found farther north. It needs a cool root zone, acidic soil, and the kind of lingering snowmelt moisture typical of high-elevation granite benches, so a rock garden with afternoon shade and consistent moisture suits it better than a warm, dry border. Grow it alongside other high-elevation heaths and dwarf conifers for an authentic Sierra timberline planting. It resents hot, humid summers and poorly drained soil, both of which quickly kill it.
sources: Rock Garden Quarterly (North American Rock Garden Society)

subcategory: native subalpine and alpine cushion perennial

planting.note: Sow seed directly into a gritty, mineral-rich scree or trough mix as soon as the ground thaws; the dense cushion resents disturbance once rooted, so transplanting established plants is rarely successful.

directions: Clubmoss mousetail is a tight, mat-forming perennial of Sierra Nevada timberline fell-fields and rocky subalpine meadows, named for its finely divided, scale-like leaflets that resemble a clubmoss shoot more than a typical rosette. Small clusters of pale yellow to cream flowers rise just above the cushion on short stalks in mid to late summer, after the surrounding snowpack recedes. It wants a lean, fast-draining, gritty mineral soil, full sun, and the cold winters and short growing season of an alpine trough or scree bed rather than ordinary garden conditions. Overwatering or rich soil quickly causes the tight cushion to rot and open up.

planting.note: Direct-sow or set out small plugs in spring into lean, rocky, fast-draining soil; avoid mulch or fertile amendments, which encourage rot in this high-elevation mat-former.

directions: Frosted buckwheat forms a dense silver-white mat of felted, woolly leaves on exposed granite outcrops and fellfields at timberline in the Sierra Nevada, its dense pubescence reflecting intense high-elevation sun and shedding moisture. Clusters of small bright yellow flowers rise on short leafless stalks above the foliage in summer and age to rust-orange. Give it full sun, sharp drainage, and lean rocky or gravelly soil; it is adapted to a short cold-winter growing season and resents both summer humidity and wet feet. It is an excellent, low-maintenance choice for a high-elevation rock garden or scree bed once its drainage needs are met.

planting.note: Divide established tufts in spring as soon as the ground thaws, or direct-sow stratified seed into gravelly, fast-draining soil; this sedge does not tolerate soggy or heavy soils.

directions: Brewer's sedge is a short, densely tufted sedge of dry, rocky subalpine and alpine slopes and timberline meadows across the Sierra Nevada, Cascades, and Rocky Mountains, forming tight clumps of stiff, curling, grass-like foliage. Unlike most sedges it thrives in lean, fast-draining gravelly soil rather than moist ground, making it a good textural filler between rocks in a high-elevation rock garden. It wants full sun, cold winters, and minimal summer water once established, and resists being overtaken by taller companions because of its low, compact habit. Leave the dried foliage through winter for structure and trim only to remove old growth in early spring.
